item.title: Linux's file permissions are over 50 years old, and three letters still decide who can touch every file on your PC
item.itunes:title: Linux's file permissions are over 50 years old, and three letters still decide who can touch every file on your PC

If you peek deep enough into Linux, you'll often find remnants from long ago, still chugging along today. But did you know that a technology that emerged in 1971 not only lives on your Linux PC to this day, but it still does the job it was invented for? This is the story of rwx, how it came to be, and how you can check it out on your own system.

The story begins with the need for a simpler way

Things were just too complicated

To see where we arrived, we have to take a look at where we started. To do that, we need to turn the clock all the way back to the 60s. Back then, there was an operating system called Multics, and the way it decided who could access which files was a little complicated.

On a Multics system, every file contained a list of permissions. It was, essentially, like a doorman with a clipboard. Whenever someone asked to do something with the file, the OS would go down the list to check for permissions. These permissions defined each user, the project group they're part of, and their permissions. When the doorman had validated the level of access the user has, it only allows them into those parts.

It was secure, but it was also quite a burden. From an administration standpoint, ensuring each file has a proper "clipboard" to work off was a bit of a nightmare. Plus, going through this list every single time someone wanted to use a file cost memory and processing power; not something that a computer from the 60s had in droves!

Windows still uses drive letters from the 1980s, and Linux's single file tree shows what we could have had

The Windows approach is convenient, but Linux seems smarter

6
By  Tanveer Singh

Two researchers devised a simpler way to do things

Nine bits, three intents

Two researchers, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie, left Multics in 1969. They wanted a system that could handle permissions for this brand-new OS they were working on, called Unix. However, they really didn't want to use the same system Multics did; they wanted something leaner, easier on the memory, and far easier to understand.

As it turns out, they discovered that a file's clipboard didn't necessarily need the granularity of every single person and every single group with every single permission. In fact, they figured out you could do quite a lot with just nine numbers, broken up into three groups.

Here's how it worked. In the Unix Programmer's Manual from 1971, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie used base-2 mathematics to represent the levels of permission. Base-2 is a little different from our main counting system, base-10. In base-2, the first digit (on the far right) represents 1, the second is 2, and the third (on the far left) is 4. You also can't use a number higher than 1 in any position, so you're stuck with 0s and 1s, which is the binary everyone talks about when discussing how computers store data.

While we, as humans, see the number '101' and read it as one hundred, no tens, and one one (making a hundred and one), a computer using base-2 would see one four, no twos, and one one. We can then convert that into base-8 by adding up the values: a four and a one equal five, so '101' in base-8 is '5'. With these three digits, the smallest number is 000 (which is 0 in base-8) and the highest is 111 (one four, one two, and one one, equals 7 in base-8).

So, here's how Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie put that knowledge to use. They took those three digits in base-2 and assigned each one a job. The leftmost digit represents read permission, the middle is write permission, and the rightmost is execution permission. A 1 means it's allowed, and 0 means it's not allowed. So, if you saw 101, that would mean someone could read and run the file, but couldn't edit it. And because it's in base-2, you can convert that to base-8 and get the number five. So, if you gave someone 'rule five', they could read and run it, but not edit it. Rule zero allowed no access at all, and rule seven allowed for everything.

Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie then combined three of these trio numbers. The first trio is what the owner can do with the file, the second is what people in a recognised group can do, and the last is what everyone else can do.

So, if you want your owner to have full access to the file, members of a recognised group to have read and execute permissions without editing it, and everyone else to only be able to read the file, you can give the owner '111', the group '101', and everyone else '100' for a string that just reads "111 101 100." And we can convert that into the more human-friendly base-8: '754'. With just nine base-2 numbers, or three base-8 ones, the two researchers could define three levels of access for three different types of users. Very smart.

The three numbers in base-2 became known as Read, Write, and Execute, or 'rwx' for short. And those three letters defined who could access what.

I was using rsync, find, sort, and tar wrong until I learned what their flags actually do

I've been Linux'ing in hard mode

By  Joe Rice-Jones

The rwx system makes its way onto Linux

It was there from the very start

Fast-forward to 1991, and a young Linus Torvalds was creating Linux. He wanted it to be POSIX-compliant so that it worked with existing Unix tools, and that meant adopting the rwx system. So, that's exactly what he did.

While Linux security has obviously come a long way since then, you can still see the effect rwx has on your system today. If you enter "ls -l" into your terminal, the bit to the left of each line is the rwx system in action. For instance, the first line of my output reads:

drwxr-xr-x. 1 simon simon 76 Oct 5 19:26 AppImages

The seemingly random jumble of letters at the very start is rwx doing its thing, around five decades after it first hit the scene. It's made up of four parts:

  • The d at the very start tells the system that this is a directory.
  • The rwx immediately after the d are the permissions for the owner: read, write, and execute.
  • The r-x after that are the permissions for the group: read and execute, but no writing. Note how the lack of write permissions is represented by a dash where the w should go.
  • The final r-x is for everyone else, and it's, again, read and execute, but no writing.

That would translate to 111 101 101, or 755 in base-8. A much simpler method than the huge clipboard.

They're just that good!

22
By  Ayush Pande

Linux is a treasure trove of ancient tech

The next time you see something odd in a Linux terminal output, do a deep dive into what it means and how it came to be. You never know; you may stumble upon a ~50-year-old permissions system that's still going strong today!

item.title: I almost replaced these 4 Samsung apps, but now I can't imagine my phone without them
item.itunes:title: I almost replaced these 4 Samsung apps, but now I can't imagine my phone without them
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Samsung phones aren't immune to bloatware, and there are times you may replace Samsung apps simply because you want to use cross-platform alternatives. You might also dismiss a few apps as unnecessary until you try them yourself.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

This happened to me with a few Samsung apps. I had initially planned to uninstall or replace them, but then they grew on me to the point that they now feel indispensable.

I cancelled 5 expensive subscriptions thanks to these underrated Samsung apps

The best replacements were already installed.

3
By  Parth Shah

Reminder

A user-friendly task app

There are few task apps that feel as intuitive and easy to use as Samsung Reminder. The app provides you with a number of templates you can use to get acquainted with its different features, including location-based and repeating reminders. The app is so good that when a friend of mine was having trouble remembering to put their insulin away when arriving at work, I set up a reminder on his phone so that he would get a notification every time he arrived there.

My most common reminder is the one I set to remember to take my migraine medication out of the fridge. Notifications are extremely easy to set up, and the app doesn't suffer from the same bloat I encounter when using other reminder apps.

Another added benefit is the ability to set how prominent a reminder is. A Light reminder comes with a short sound and notification, a Medium one includes a full-screen alert and short sound, and a Strong reminder includes a full-screen alert and long sound.

However, the one feature I wish the app had is the ability to set a recurring reminder based on the date of completion. I use these types of reminders for chores.

My Samsung phone kept draining battery overnight, so I built this routine

My Galaxy finally sleeps properly now.

1
By  Parth Shah

Modes and Routines

Automation made easy

There are quite a few automation apps out there, but what makes Modes and Routines special is how easy it is to use. This is by far one of the most beginner-friendly ways to start with automation, while also giving the user an extensive number of triggers and actions they can try.

You can even add further functionality by adding Routines+, one of my must-have Good Lock plugins. This plugin adds Just In routines, as well as automations tied to the side key on your phone. Currently, I have my lower volume key set to open my weather app, for example.

Modes and Routines includes a Discover page with plenty of example routines that you can use as-is or tweak slightly to your own needs. I like to use this page to get ideas about potential new routines to create. This is honestly a feature that I wish more smartphone manufacturers would include on their devices, since it unlocks the automation capabilities of your smartphone without requiring additional accessories.

Samsung Keyboard

A Good Lock plugin unlocks precise customization

When it comes to keyboard apps, I've had a strong preference for Microsoft SwiftKey for years. This means I would usually switch the native keyboard on a phone to SwiftKey instead. However, Samsung Keyboard changed that, and it's because of a specific Good Lock module — Keys Cafe.

With Keys Cafe, I can customize my Samsung Keyboard to suit my preferences exactly. This goes beyond the customization of other keyboard apps and lets me design a theme that fits my tastes while also catering to my light sensitivity.

Since Good Lock is a Samsung app and only customizes Samsung Keyboard, it turned the native Galaxy app into a must-have on my S23 Ultra. Whenever I use a keyboard on another device, I miss the colors and effects that come with my Samsung version.

I turned my Galaxy home screen into something I actually enjoy looking at with these 5 tricks

Your home screen doesn't have to be generic.

By  Megan Ellis

Clock

My persistent, but flexible, alarm app

I'm so reliant on Samsung's Clock app that even if I'm not using my Samsung phone as my daily driver, I make sure that I always have the device around to wake me up in the morning.

This comes down to the flexibility of the app, especially with its snooze function. It gives me a maximum snooze period of one hour, which suits my sleeping patterns well. I have chronic fatigue, so waking up in the morning is a constant struggle. The long snooze time gives me extra time to rest when I simply can't get up. At the same time, I can adjust the snooze when the alarm goes off, which is great when I just need an extra 10 minutes.

More recently, Samsung added the ability to create groups of alarms, allowing you to turn all alarms in a group on or off at once. This is another feature that works well for my own habits.

One UI is quietly killing your Samsung battery — here's which 6 settings to disable

Find out which unexpected OneUI features are secretly draining your Galaxy phone's battery and how to disable them.

By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

Give your pre-installed Galaxy apps a chance to see if you find something great

Our phones often come with bloatware, and there are definitely Samsung apps worth uninstalling or disabling if you don't use them. But not every pre-installed app is a gimmick or unnecessary addition — there are some great features hiding in apps you've overlooked.

The main drawback is that if you switch to a different smartphone brand, you can't bring these apps with you. But if you're a Samsung Galaxy loyalist, that's not a problem at all.

item.title: I missed the days of channel surfing, so I recreated the experience with Jellyfin
item.itunes:title: I missed the days of channel surfing, so I recreated the experience with Jellyfin
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
As a kid, I absolutely loved channel surfing. I never knew what I might stumble across, and the joy of discovering a new TV show was half the fun. I remember one night, I stumbled across a channel showing anime I'd never heard of before.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

For a kid whose knowledge of anime extended solely to what appeared on Toonami or Adult Swim, that was a huge win (and it birthed a lifelong love of Slayers). Nowadays, that experience is long gone. Everything is on-demand through streaming platforms, which means I basically always know what I'm going to find. I might not know if I'll like a show, but I at least have some idea of what it is before I start watching.

Ersatz.tv let me change that by allowing me to create my own channel lineup that I can flip through. It's a bit like Spelunkr.tv, another service that's growing in popularity, but it's based entirely on my Jellyfin server (and doesn't have chat features or audience reactions, which I cannot stress enough how much I appreciate). Ersatz.tv links to a variety of platforms, including Jellyfin, Emby, and Plex, so you can recapture that nostalgic experience you grew up with.

ErsatzTV turns my Jellyfin library into my personal cable network

I can create channels from the media I already own

I have a lot of older TV shows in my Jellyfin library. Titles like Friends, How I Met Your Mother, Psych, and so on. These are comfort shows — content I like to keep on in the background while I'm cleaning the house or doing dishes. ErsatzTV allows me to create a channel that's just these shows, with episodes playing in random order, in set time blocks that follow the structure of cable TV.

ErsatzTV provides the framework, but I provide the content. You can install Ersatz in multiple ways, including prebuilt binary packages or Docker. Connecting it to your media server is as simple as grabbing the correct API key. I figured that, since it was so easy to connect the two, my content would appear right away, but I found that syncing the content was a separate step.

Although ErsatzTV can detect your Jellyfin server, it can't access any content until you sync the libraries you want. I almost missed that step. Here's how to do it, using Jellyfin as an example. After you've added your Jellyfin API key to ErsatzTV, select Jellyfin in the left-hand menu. It's a subcategory of Media Sources.

Once selected, click the Play button icon on the far right of the screen, between the refresh and folder icons. This opens a menu showing every top-level library on your Jellyfin server. Click the toggle on the right side of the screen, beneath Synchronize, and then click the Save Changes button just below the search bar. After that, your content should begin appearing in ErsatzTV. Give it 10 to 15 minutes, depending on your library size.

Creating a channel was more involved than I expected

Channels and schedules are separate pieces of the puzzle

The fun starts once you move past the initial connection phase. That's when you can begin setting up custom channels in ErsatzTV, but this isn't as straightforward as it initially seemed. The channels work in tandem with schedules to create that cable TV experience. I enjoyed playing around with it, but I spent a lot of time in menus before I saw results.

What threw me off was that creating a channel didn't actually let me select what I wanted to play. I had to create a schedule, select the shows I wanted to include, and then assign that schedule to a specific channel using a layout. None of the steps are particularly difficult to do, but they aren't immediately apparent when first using ErsatzTV.

Several scheduling options are available, such as "Shuffle," which randomizes content without repeating it until everything has played, or "Season, Episode," which plays a TV series from start to finish in proper order. You can do a lot with this, like building a channel to play holiday movies or one dedicated solely to your favorite anime genre.

Once I had that set up, I had to make the channel actually play. I added the newly created channels to Jellyfin. ErsatzTV provides the M3U playlist for Jellyfin's tuner, plus an XMLTV feed for the program guide. This gives you that classic TV guide channel where you can look to see what's currently playing.

The end result brings back something streaming services lost

Sometimes, I just want to watch TV without choosing what to watch

While ErsatzTV isn't likely to surprise me with a new show — after all, I know what's in my Jellyfin library — it can give me something to watch that doesn't require any conscious effort on my part. Well, after the setup, anyway. Sometimes, I just want to turn on the TV and watch something without spending too long trying to decide what sounds good.

Randomizing the programming means I can find something interesting I wasn't specifically looking for, like maybe an old show I haven't seen in years. It helps to wipe the digital dust off my Jellyfin server, so to speak.

I connected my HD antenna to a cheap tuner, and now I can watch free TV anywhere in my house

With a refurbished tuner and HD Antenna, I get OTA live TV everywhere.

Channel surfing is fun again

ErsatzTV is an awesome tool, but it's definitely one I'd only suggest to enthusiasts. You'll spend a fair bit of time getting it set up, and it can be pretty confusing to understand. But if you push through that (and the extensive documentation helps a lot), you'll find yourself with a nostalgic experience I thought Netflix had killed.

item.title: PETG is the filament I'd tell every beginner to start with instead of PLA
item.itunes:title: PETG is the filament I'd tell every beginner to start with instead of PLA
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I first got into 3D printing, I didn't pay much heed to the tiny spool of black PLA filament shipped with most entry-level printers. The first Benchy and calibration cubes were made out of it, but I'd gotten into the hobby of fabricating functional parts that solve everyday hardware problems around my home and garage, and I wasn't the only beginner with these expectations. Using PLA for functional prints undermines this goal immediately with a low tolerance to heat and brittle failure modes.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I've since relegated PLA to printing desk trinkets, display figurines, and calibration Benchys. I have since switched my default spool to glycol-modified polyethylene terephthalate (PETG) and finally got the durable, real-world output that justifies owning a desktop machine. It's now integral to my advice for beginners. Sure, it takes more slicer tuning and flow adjustment along with a good print bed, but your prints will last a long time. 3D printing demands a time and effort investment unlike any other hobby, but PETG is worthwhile because you'll get tough, weather-capable hardware that works outside your four walls.

Why PETG survives real-world loads and heat where PLA fails

Two important mechanical parameters that do all the explaining

My outdoor EV charging gun holder proved to me why PETG belongs on every beginner's spool holder from the start. That wall-mounted bracket carries the daily weight of a heavy insulated charging cable, absorbs repeated impacts every time I dock the connector, and bakes in afternoon ambient heat. Anecdotal reports across the maker community warn against putting PLA under sustained mechanical stress or outdoor warmth, and material testing confirmed why my first holster printed in PLA failed in that environment.

However, PETG isn't universally stronger than PLA, because strength depends on mechanical metrics you measure. Controlled pull and bending tests by Stefan Hermann at CNC Kitchen, along with material comparisons from 3D printer manufacturers, show that standard PLA beats PETG in raw static tensile strength — posting roughly 55 to 65 MPa compared to PETG's 45 to 55 MPa—and offers higher bending stiffness.

However, high stiffness without compliance turns PLA into a liability for working parts. If loads exceed layer adhesion strength or the material limits, the polymer shatters without warning. In stark contrast, PETG has around thrice PLA's impact toughness (8 to 12 kJ/m² versus PLA's 2 to 4 kJ/m²), higher elongation at break making it ideal for snap-fit tabs, and superior inter-layer adhesion that resists shock loads.

5 filaments that are better than PLA for serious 3D printing projects

While PLA definitely fills the 3D printing needs for many projects, other filament materials are better for more serious projects

8
By  Jeff Butts

Thermal endurance widens the gap even further when your prints leave climate-controlled rooms. PLA reaches its glass transition temperature between 55°C and 60°C, meaning it loses structural stiffness in a parked summer car or on a sun-facing wall. PETG pushes that glass transition threshold up to 75°C–85°C and resists sustained ultraviolet exposure much better, hitting the sweet spot for outdoor brackets and non-critical automotive accessories you might want to print.

Choosing the right build plate goes a long way

3D printing has many variables, but this is the biggest with PETG

Beginners who jump straight into PETG without checking their build surface learn an expensive lesson on their very first print. While PLA releases politely from almost any cooled plate, molten PETG forms a fierce chemical bond with bare smooth polyetherimide (PEI) sheets and untempered glass. The copolymer rips chunks of PEI straight off the spring steel when you pull the finished print off. Avoiding bed damage takes ten seconds of preparation.

Both the Prusa Knowledge Base and the Bambu Lab Wiki recommend pairing PETG with a powder-coated textured PEI plate or a satin build sheet, where the micro-texture prevents a vacuum-tight molecular weld and lets parts pop loose automatically once the bed cools below 35°C. If you only own a smooth PEI sheet, a glass bed, or a G10 Garolite plate, you could wipe on a thin sacrificial release layer of PVA glue or ammonia-based glass cleaner before heating the bed. Pair that prep with a 230°C–250°C nozzle and a slower part cooling fan for a solid first layer with excellent interlayer fusion.

PETG isn't immune to the environment

At least not until you print with it, that is

Recommending PETG does not mean ignoring its annoyances at the hot end. PETG is aggressively hygroscopic, pulling humidity out of the room air two to three times faster than PLA. The results of moist spools suffer from foamy walls and aggressive stringing across traversals without commanded extrusion. I would honestly reach for PLA far more often if I did not have a filament dryer working alongside my printer.

Baking PETG spools at 60°C to 65°C for six hours before a print — and storing them in sealed desiccant boxes afterward — eliminates moisture-induced oozing at the root. Baking PETG spools at 60°C to 65°C for six hours before a print — and storing them in sealed desiccant boxes afterward — eliminates moisture-induced oozing, and a $45 dryer with your first printer sets you up for printing with way more materials than just PETG.

It helps if you plan to fabricate load-bearing brackets rather than plastic toys. Beyond drying, I always calibrate a dedicated slicer profile for each manufacturer's filament and individual color, because the typical titanium dioxide in white spools or heavy pigments in translucent blends shift viscosity and optimal nozzle temperature by 10°C to 15°C.

I tried ABS on my budget 3D printer and realized the difficulty is mostly myth

ABS fumes are still a problem, though

1
By  Ayush Pande

At times PLA is better, but PETG is better for starters

Even as a committed PETG advocate, I still keep a few spools of PLA on hand for projects where PETG's sticky, viscous melt works against it. PLA's surface detail for tabletop miniatures, long unsupported bridges, and high stiffness deliver cleaner geometry at faster print speeds. Its ease of use makes it ideal for testing after machine geometry adjustments and for decorative indoor models that never face a drop or a warm window.

However, in 3D printing, moisture control, build-surface matching, and per-material profile tuning are vital skills better built early, and not just for working with PETG. Dial those fundamentals in the first week, and every print thereafter can confidently hold loads, survive summers in your backyard, or drop on the floor without shattering. After all, functional prints are a big reason why you bought that 3D printer.

item.title: Prebuilt NAS boxes are underpowered for the price, so I built one with a desktop CPU instead
item.itunes:title: Prebuilt NAS boxes are underpowered for the price, so I built one with a desktop CPU instead
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Building a DIY network-attached storage (NAS) solution that beats prebuilt enclosures isn't terribly challenging. Well, it didn't used to be. With the price of PC parts these days, it's anything but. That's why we put together a new tool to help you save money when building desktop PCs, home servers, NAS, and other devices. We're proud of this new platform, and so I decided to give it a go and see if it could provide a configuration for a NAS to store 5TB of data and run some apps, all for less than $1,000.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

XDB Builder managed it, but only just. Taking away the 6TB HDD, the NAS build would cost less than $650. Fancy building this NAS yourself? Go for it! Here's the XDB Builder link.

Why bother building your own NAS?

Prebuilt enclosures are great, but DIY is much better

I love Synology, TerraMaster, Asustor, and other branded NAS enclosures. I believe they offer excellent platforms for those new to the wonderful world of NAS to get started with very little in the form of an onboarding process. With a custom PC-come-NAS, you need to put together the system, install an OS, get it all working together in harmony, and then carry out maintenance and troubleshooting. Prebuilt enclosures come with warranty and support channels, and everything is essentially managed for you. But this limits choice, and there's a premium to pay.

For my example NAS build, I need to store 5TB worth of data (or thereabouts). I also want to use the NAS as a small home server, running a few self-hosted apps. Think Nextcloud, Jellyfin, Immich, Mealie, and a few other lighter services. On the prebuilt front, one would have to spend at least $400 to pick up an enclosure with enough horsepower and the relevant specifications. I'd need a four-bay NAS at the very least, and an Intel CPU would be a must-have for transcoding and other requirements. The Synology DiskStation DS925+ is amazing, but it costs $640.

TerraMaster usually undercuts everyone in the business, but even its own F4-425 starts from around $500, and that's for an Intel N5095. It's great for saving a little on running costs, but it's severely underpowered compared to something like an Intel Core i5 CPU you'd find inside a desktop PC. That's precisely what XDB Builder recommended with its configuration.

Meet the XDB Builder NAS

It's quite the compelling storage solution

Powered by an Intel Core i5-14400 CPU with 10 physical cores, this NAS build doesn't mess around. Running virtual machines (VMs) and Linux containers (LXCs) will be a non-issue. We've got a basic ASRock B760M Pro-A/D4 to match the chip, which is absolutely fine thanks to the two full-size PCI slots, four RAM slots, and four SATA III ports. We can add a GPU later or rely on the Intel UHD Graphics and install two PCI SATA expansion cards for even more HDDs.

One thing I had to swap out was the 1TB SSD the build tool decided to add to the mix. We need to store a lot of data, and I wanted to create the challenge by limiting the budget to $1,000 and not a penny more. The 8TB Seagate IronWolf HDD is a perfect match for storing lots of data, and it's also the most expensive component of the build, coming in at a whopping $424. Check it out and see what you think! I opted for the Fractal Design Define 7, though any mid-tower or full-tower with HDD bays will do.

Intel Core i5 14400

Motherboard

ASRock B760M Pro-A/D4

RAM

Mushkin Redline ST 16GB (2x8GB) DDR4-4000

Storage

Seagate IronWolf 8TB

Intenso Top 256GB

PSU

Corsair CX600

Case

Fractal Design Define 7 Black

Total cost

$1071

Originally, 64GB of RAM was configured by the tool, which was actually a rather smart move. I specified that I'd run a few apps on here for self-hosting, and that would require containers with memory allocation. The thing is, I don't want to spend too much on the build, and RAM is incredibly expensive right now. 16GB (two 8GB modules) is perfectly serviceable. We can double this up to 32GB to take advantage of all four DIMM slots. All of this for around $1,000 is not too bad at all.

One thing to note with using PC parts is the type of storage used matters more than you may initially believe. Standard consumer-grade storage drives from older PCs will happily store all your data on the network, but these aren't typically rated for continuous operation. There's a notable difference between running your desktop for a full day and running a NAS operating non-stop for months, sometimes years. This produces wear on moving parts, which HDDs have a few. If repurposing old storage, always run SMART checks (and then some).

Try creating some builds today

We're still messing with the sliders in the background and seeing what works (and what breaks). When looking at building a new DIY NAS, using some existing parts, or considering a prebuilt enclosure, give XDB Builder a go and see what you think. It may just provide some insight to what it takes to run a NAS and home server from the same machine using nothing but off-the-shelf parts. Turnkey enclosures have their place and are a solid choice for beginners, but DIY is the way to go when you're ready for the next stage.

item.title: I decluttered my desk, and this 6-port 240W charging station is the only one I use now
item.itunes:title: I decluttered my desk, and this 6-port 240W charging station is the only one I use now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have way too many gadgets on my desk, and charging is sometimes a hassle. I have dozens of GaN chargers, and while they're small and don't take up much room, most have only three or four ports. Then there are charging stations like the UGREEN Nexode 500W; while I use one in the office, it's too big and unwieldy for my desk.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That's where Satechi's ChargeView 240W comes in. It's a six-port charging station, but it is considerably smaller than most of its rivals, and it has a must-have feature I need in any charger I use now: a built-in LCD panel. The panel shows real-time charging info — including how much wattage is going out of each port — and takes all the guesswork out of knowing just how long it takes to charge a connected device.

The best part? You get six USB-C ports. Most charging stations I use have one USB-A port, and while I still need (and use) USB-A cables, they're no longer a priority, so having a charger with just USB-C ports makes things easier for me. Now, if you don't need six ports, Satechi also has a smaller ChargeView model with four ports and a total power budget of 140W. I tested that in the past as well, and given my charging needs, I prefer the 240W model. The ChargeView 240W retails for $149, and the ChargeView 140W is $99 as of writing.

I stopped charging my phone through my car's USB port after making one simple upgrade

I switched to a 12V USB-C charger in my car, and my phone never drains again

32
By  Dhruv Bhutani

This charger has power to spare

With USB PD 3.2 and a 240W power budget, this is a desk charger with a difference

Let's talk about what you're getting with the ChargeView 240W. The charging station has six USB-C ports, but they're not the same; the USB-C1 and C2 ports are based on the USB PD 3.2 protocol and go up to 140W and have AVS. These ports are ideal if you're looking to charge a Googlebook, a power bank, iPhone 18 Pro Max, or other phones. The USB-C3 and C4 ports use the USB PD 3.0 standard and go up to 100W individually, and the C5/C6 ports also leverage USB PD 3.0, but only hit 30W each.

Build quality is quite good. The charging station is made of plastic, and like all other Satechi products I have used in the last three years, there are no problems with long-term durability. The front fascia has a glossy coat, and it hasn't picked up too many scratches after plugging and unplugging USB-C cables a few hundred times. The bundled power cable is 1.5 meters, but you will need a longer cable if you're like me and use a standing desk.

Satechi has a smart power distribution algorithm that dynamically changes how much power devices get when more than one port is in active use. If you're using the USB-C1 and C2 ports at the same time, C1 gets 140W, with C2 dropping to a maximum of 100W. With three ports in use (C1, C2, and C3), it goes to 100W + 100W + 40W to hit the 240W ceiling, and with four ports (C1, C2, C3, and C4), that goes down to 100W + 70W + 40W + 30W. With all but the C6 ports in use, you're looking at 100W + 70W + 30W + 20W + 20W. And finally, with all six ports in active use, you get 70W + 70W + 30W + 30W + 20W + 20W.

You can easily charge everything

The ChargeView 240W is great for just about every device

I tested the ChargeView 240W with the Pixel 11 Pro XL, iPhone 18 Pro Max, Vivo X500 Pro Max, Find X10 Pro Max, Xiaomi 17 Ultra, and a dozen other phones in the three months I used it, and it did a great job delivering a reliable charge to connected devices. I also used it with a slew of 165W and 200W power banks with USB PD 3.1, and it charged these products at 140W consistently. I didn't see much in the way of overheating, and the smaller design combined with the built-in panel makes it a great choice if you're looking for a desk charger to use with all of your gadgets.

What I also like is the ability to change orientation. The ChargeView 240W comes with a stand, and you can easily change the orientation to vertical or horizontal. I used it in horizontal mode as it sat just underneath my work monitor, but if you're putting it on the side, a vertical orientation is a better choice. Oh, and the panel changes based on the orientation, so that's good to see.

The only thing missing is Qi2 charging. This is one of the reasons I used Baseus' Nomos 245W charger in the past; it was convenient to just plonk the iPhone 18 Pro Max or the Pixel 11 Pro XL on the Qi 2 mat and let it charge. Sure, it isn't as fast as plugging in the devices, but it's much more convenient, and the Qi2 pad doubles as a phone stand, giving me yet another reason to use it. That feature isn't available on the ChargeView 240W, and Satechi needs to consider adding it with the next iteration.

Overall, the ChargeView 240W has proven to be one of the best charging stations around. It's smaller than the UGREEN and Baseus chargers I used in the past, does a great job charging all of my devices, and has a panel that shows real-time charging info. Outside of Qi2, there isn't much missing here, and it's a good choice if you need an all-in-one charging station.

item.title: I use Obsidian to manage my entire business, and I barely need other apps
item.itunes:title: I use Obsidian to manage my entire business, and I barely need other apps
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Running a business means managing projects, tracking deadlines, organizing client information, brainstorming ideas, and keeping important documents within reach. I had a separate app for almost everything, and switching between them was a nightmare.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That’s when I decided to take a different approach and turn Obsidian into my business command center. With the right folder structure, plugins, templates, and a few clever workflows, I have managed to replace several dedicated business tools without sacrificing much functionality.

3 free Obsidian plugins I use to automate my entire vault

My Obsidian vault practically runs itself.

By  Parth Shah

I built my own business dashboard

Everything important is one click away

The first thing I wanted was a central dashboard that would give me a complete overview of my business without jumping between notes and folders. I created a dedicated home note in Obsidian and turned it into my personal business headquarters.

Instead of starting at a long list of Markdown files, I now have a neatly organized dashboard with quick links to my active projects, clients, upcoming deadlines, financial records, meeting notes, and important resources.

I used Obsidian’s native callouts, internal links, and embedded notes to organize everything into different sections. For example, I have a dedicated area for ongoing projects, a section for important business notes, and another for my daily priorities. I can jump straight into my editorial calendar, review pending assignments, or open a client’s profile with a single click.

My entire setup is flexible. I can rearrange sections, add new shortcuts, and expand my dashboard as my business grows. I don’t need to deal with complicated widgets or pay for a premium dashboard builder.

Bases handle my entire project pipeline

My projects finally have proper structure

Obsidian Bases has changed how I manage my business projects. Instead of maintaining separate spreadsheets or relying on apps like Trello and Notion, I can create structured databases right inside my vault. I use properties like project name, client, priority, deadline, and status to keep everything organized.

The best part is that Bases now supports Kanban boards, which makes tracking complex projects much more convenient.

For example, if I am working on a complex Swami Jewels website, I can break the entire project into smaller tasks and arrange them as cards under different columns, such as To Do, In Progress, Review, and Completed.

From designing the homepage and building product pages to testing the checkout process, every task gets its own card. As work progresses, I drag cards between columns to update their status.

I can use Bases to manage my editorial calendar, track client deliverables, monitor upcoming deadlines, or maintain a database of business expenses.

All this information remains connected to my existing Obsidian notes. I don’t need to maintain another project management app just to keep track of what’s happening across my business.

My client information stays organized

A lightweight CRM without monthly fees

Managing multiple clients can quickly become a headache, especially when their contact details, project requirements, meeting notes, and important conversations are scattered across different apps. Instead of paying for a dedicated CRM solution, I decided to build a lightweight client management system inside Obsidian.

I created a dedicated Clients folder where every client gets their own note with essential information, ongoing projects, deadlines, and other relevant details.

I also use Bases to create a structured client directory where I can filter by project status, priority, or upcoming deadlines. With templates (more on that in a minute), adding a new client takes just a few clicks, and I can maintain a consistent structure across all profiles.

Of course, Obsidian doesn’t offer the advanced sales automation and communication features of a full-fledged CRM. However, for keeping track of client relationships, project histories, and everyday business information, it does the job well.

4 game-changing Obsidian workflows I wish I tried earlier

Obsidian workflows I tried late, but you don’t have to

4
By  Parth Shah

Canvas is my brainstorming headquarters

Templates and automation eliminate repetitive work

I have also replaced dedicated brainstorming tools like Miro with Obsidian Canvas. Whenever I am planning a complex website, brainstorming business ideas, or mapping out a new project, I open Canvas and start arranging notes, images, and cards on an infinite whiteboard.

Also, I don’t want to waste time creating the same document structure or manually organizing notes every day. That’s why I have combined Obsidian’s Templates feature with the AutoMover plugin to automate repetitive tasks.

For example, I have ready-made templates for client profiles, project briefs, meeting notes, software reviews, and weekly reviews. Whenever I start a new project, I apply the relevant template and fill in the details.

AutoMover takes things a step further by automatically organizing my notes based on predefined rules. I can configure it to move notes into specific folders depending on their filenames or tags. For instance, notes tagged #client can automatically land in my Clients folder, while project-related notes move to a designated location.

I can also create exclusion rules to prevent unwanted changes. Check out my dedicated post to learn more about AutoMover plugin for Obsidian.

I never expected Obsidian to scale

I never imagined that a simple Markdown-based note-taking app could become the backbone of my entire business. Yet with a customized dashboard, Bases, Canvas, client management, and a handful of templates, Obsidian has replaced several tools I once considered essential.

Of course, Obsidian isn’t a complete replacement for specialized accounting, communication, or invoicing software, and setting everything up takes some effort. But for managing my everyday business operations, it comes quite close.

item.title: I gave my ESP32 a second job as an RF analyzer, and now I'm not buying a dedicated spectrum monitor
item.itunes:title: I gave my ESP32 a second job as an RF analyzer, and now I'm not buying a dedicated spectrum monitor
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When a remote, sensor, or smart-home device acts up, I usually can’t tell why. I can’t tell whether the device is failing, its antenna is poorly placed, or something nearby is interfering with it . An RF analyzer can help investigate these problems by showing activity across different frequencies and the strength of received signals.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

A benchtop one seemed excessive for occasional experiments. So I built one from the parts I already had: an $8 ESP32-S3 microcontroller and a sub-$5 CC1101 wireless transceiver module. I used an open-source project called BKFZ SubGHz to scan the radio spectrum and view the results in a browser on my computer. This isn't professional-grade equipment, but it gives me an accessible way to explore sub-GHz radio activity around my home.

4 ESP32 projects that need nothing more than the board and a USB cable

You don't need extra sensors just to build a couple of ESP32 projects

1
By  Ayush Pande

Using CC1101 for RF work that my ESP32 can’t handle

The microcontroller sweeps while the transceiver listens

The ESP32-S3 is my go-to board because it has enough memory to run code, plus Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity. However, its built-in wireless radios operate in the 2.4GHz band and can’t directly tune into the sub-GHz frequencies used in wireless sensors and remotes. The CC1101 supports these frequency ranges:

  • 300MHz to 348MHz
  • 387MHz to 464MHz
  • 779MHz to 928MHz

These are the tuning ranges the module supports, but actual performance also depends on its RF circuitry and antenna.

The module reports the RSSI (received signal strength) value, which is the foundation of this project. I can use ESP32 to build a visual representation of radio activity in the selected band after running the receiver across a range of frequencies and recording the readings.

CC1101 modules are sold in 433 MHz and 868/915 MHz variants. Their antennas should match the frequency band you want to explore, so check the module and antenna specifications before you buy one. I set the S3 to a frequency (433MHz); the CC1101 swings into action to read the RSSI values. I used the hardware wiring table on the SmartRC C1101 Driver library’s GitHub page, but modified the GPIO pins to suit the S3.

ESP32-S3

ESP32-S3 comes with a dual-core Xtensa LX7 microcontroller. It comes in varations up to 16MB of flash memory and 8MB of PSRAM with years of maturity to be ready for a variety of projects.

See at Amazon

I can see radio activity from my laptop using an ESP32

Setup involves pins, a config line, and LittleFS upload

BKFZ SubGHz is an open-source project by brianwalczak that uses the ELECHOUSE_CC1101_SRC_DRV library to control the CC1101. It also uses ESPAsyncWebServer to serve a browser-based interface, with WebSocket communication handling the data exchange. Its Frequency Analyzer scans supported frequencies and visualizes the readings. The project’s README states that any ESP32 will do, but its default pins are set for classic ESP32 boards. However, I used an ESP32-S3, so I had to remap the SPI pins in the configuration files to match my board.

BKFZ SubGHz defaults to Bluetooth connectivity, but I switched the connection to Wi-Fi by changing the CONNECTION_MODE definition to CONNECTION_MODE_WIFI. The Wi-Fi interface also needs its supporting files, so I installed the LittleFS Upload plugin for Arduino IDE and uploaded the project’s data/ directory to the ESP32’s filesystem. Then, I flashed the firmware using Arduino IDE.

Once the S3 boots, it creates its own Wi-Fi AP called BKFZ SubGHz. I connected my laptop to that network, opened 192.168.4.1 in a browser, and hit Connect to view the interface and graphs. The browser then gives me access to the project’s interface, including its Frequency Analyzer, without requiring a separate mobile app or an internet connection.

I walked around my house to see how radio signals changed

The same frequency looked different in every room

I started the device in a room with no phones or other devices transmitting nearby to establish a baseline. Then I checked the 433MHz frequency, which is common for remotes, doorbells, and wireless sensors. These devices often transmit in short bursts, so a frequency sweep can miss them entirely. That’s what I learned after double-checking my build, since it didn’t show any data initially. So I repeatedly pressed remote buttons while scanning to see whether the receiver picked up their transmissions.

The readings changed, although I couldn’t attribute the peaks to the remote presses without identifying the signals and verifying their frequencies first. Moving the antenna around also changed the readings. Radio signals reflect off walls and furniture, so even a small shift in antenna position affects reception. I kept the antenna in the same spot when comparing readings between rooms.

This isn’t a replacement for professional RF equipment

Short transmissions and interference are difficult to catch

The RSSI value estimates received signal strength, not a fully calibrated power measurement. I wouldn’t use this project to certify a wireless device or check regulatory emissions. Beyond missing short bursts, the CC1101 can also struggle with strong nearby signals. Without adequate filtering ahead of its receiver, a sufficiently strong signal can overload the front end and produce unreliable readings. Even for that, you'll need to tweak the original sketch to make it work with your particular ESP32 board and Wi-Fi.

As mentioned earlier, an antenna designed for 433MHz won’t perform particularly well at 868MHz or 915MHz. This is another reason to avoid treating the readings as absolute measurements. I only used the analyzer to listen, even though the firmware supports transmitting. Transmission power limits, permitted frequencies, and operating conditions vary by country. I can still check if a remote produces a detectable signal and compare the readings between rooms.

A decent setup to troubleshoot the RF spectrum at home

This ESP32-based project is best viewed as a hobbyist tool for exploring the sub-GHz spectrum in your home. It takes some tinkering with the wiring and firmware, but you can always buy a ready-to-use instrument, like a tinySA. A dedicated analyzer comes with a display and requires no firmware flashing or custom wiring. That said, it costs more than reusing the components you already own.

item.itunes:title: I compared 4K Blu-ray to regular Blu-ray, and the difference was smaller than I expected
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I recently ran a test comparing an upscaled DVD on my Nvidia Shield to 4K streaming, and the results were intriguing. It was a closer contest than I expected; I knew I couldn't watch streaming without seeing compression artifacts. When it comes to media, we want the best quality possible.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

But I don't assume something is better just because we're told it is. So, I was curious about the quality and price difference between a UHD 4K and a standard (non-upscaled) Blu-ray disc. Is the difference big enough to justify $10-15 more per disc and gigs of server space?

Creating a uniform comparison

Same movie, TV, and Blu-ray player setting adjustments

I chose a movie from the MCU because it has spectacular visuals, color, and detail. I picked Spider-Man: Far From Home since I've seen it enough times to know what to look for in key scenes. I played both discs on the same Panasonic DP-UB820 UHD Blu-ray player through a Vizio 4K TV. I also kept the same TV settings to avoid skewing my anecdotal test. I restored the TV's settings to default and used the TV's default calibrated dark setting with no other picture adjustments.

Another issue I had to address is that my Blu-ray player upscales standard Blu-ray discs to 4K by default, which is a nice feature, but not for this test. So I went into its settings and changed the resolution from 4K to 1080p. I switched the player's output to standard Blu-ray and left the TV to handle scaling to fit the 3840×2160 pixel resolution display. I wanted to ensure I was getting the full visual experience of the 1080p Blu-ray without upscaling getting in the way.

I did this test with the actual discs and not Blu-ray rips. I wanted to ensure I was using the full amount of data each disc contains to compare picture and sound quality. Even a properly ripped MakeMKV Blu-ray remux copies the disc's audio and video without re-encoding, but server and network issues can still affect quality. Transcoding, tone-mapping, and network issues can affect playback. Using physical discs, the same player and TV kept the playback devices consistent without introducing media servers.

Regular Blu-ray looks great

The movie on the disc was impressive

After adjusting my player's settings, I watched the full movie starting on the standard Blu-ray at its native resolution. It looked good. For a Marvel flick, the colors popped, scenes were clean and tight, and the movie was enjoyable. It certainly didn't have grainy DVD quality. I wasn't thinking about what I might be missing, and I never felt the urge to pop in the 4K UHD disc while I watched.

The 4K Blu-ray looked better, but a standard Blu-ray is no slouch

It wasn't a way better experience in 4K

When I popped in the UHD 4K disc after watching the standard Blu-ray version, I was expecting it to look better, and it did. However, it wasn't a magical new experience that made me never want to watch a 1080p disc again. I remember the jump from DVD to Blu-ray, and it was a major contrast in quality. A standard Blu-ray already displays detailed textures, colors, and clear images, which gives UHD something to build on. But the quality difference between standard Blu-ray and UHD isn't there.

Blu-ray.com gave this disc a five-star rating for audio and video. Still, it's worth comparing versions to see whether a standard disc is good enough. I'm glad I did this test and found that, at least for modern movies, it might be enough.

I can rip the Blu-ray and replace the 4K files. I will need to see how standard Blu-ray rips perform, but if they hold up, I can start saving on storage. I won't go as far as only buying standard Blu-ray. But if I can spend less on server storage and keep my library, it's a win.

I automated my Blu-ray ripping setup, and now building my movie library costs next to nothing

I don't need to break the bank for storage

5
By  Jasmine Mannan

Standard Blu-ray is great, and a cheaper solution in many ways

If you don't have a super high-resolution TV set, a standard Blu-ray looks great. Unless you're a videophile, even on a TV with incredible resolution, you won't notice the difference until you watch the versions back-to-back. The bottom line is a modern, properly transferred standard Blu-ray is great, but 4K does look better. But it isn't as impressive as the leap from DVD to Blu-ray.

Now, I'm rethinking how I rip and replace files in my media library. Or at least re-encode 4K rips. I'm not going all in on standard Blu-ray. Future-proof media and having choice is nice. But storage is at a premium, and prices aren't going down anytime soon.

item.itunes:title: I stopped copying ISOs to my Ventoy drive because this free tool lets me boot operating systems over the network
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I frequently install operating systems, which means downloading the latest ISO files. Whether it's Windows, a Linux distribution, or a tool, you first need to download it and then write it to a USB drive. Rufus is a great tool to do so, but recreating a bootable USB drive is tedious. Ventoy lets you keep multiple ISO files for any OS or tool on a single bootable USB drive. I have one such drive with ten useful tools and ISO files of my commonly used operating systems.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

But even USB drives or an SSD have a fixed storage space. You cannot just copy everything onto it and only have to keep the most necessary ones. I recently tried a tool that doesn't force you to download an ISO file beforehand to install the OS. It handles everything and makes me question the future of my Ventoy USB.

Ventoy is a great tool

But you can't put everything on one drive

My Ventoy drive has 28GB of available storage space, and Ubuntu, Windows 11, Windows 10, and two MX Linux distributions occupy most of it. I could use a bigger drive, but that won't get me the distro variety I need when I want to install on someone else's system. Ventoy can even run from an SSD, but in this expensive storage era, you have to be mindful.

I would prefer using the SSD for something more useful. It can serve as an OS installation drive rather than storing a bunch of ISO files. ISO files can also become outdated, and you have to download newer versions when they are released. So, what's the alternative? Network boot.

My Linux desktop fits on a USB drive, and it boots the same on any PC I use

My full setup, wherever I go

12
By  João Carrasqueira

The concept has been around for a while, and I use netboot.xyz. It uses iPXE to connect to its own server, from which it can fetch installers, live environments, and a few more resources for multiple operating systems. So your Ventoy drives stay lean, and you only need one tool to install multiple OS and their variants.

Netboot.xyz has a diverse range of options

Moderate setup complexity

Whenever you think of a network-based tool with no graphical interface, you question how easy it is to use. I was also skeptical of using it because when you load such tools, they need to identify your installed hardware. You can create a dedicated USB drive for netboot.xyz, but I prefer keeping it on the Ventoy drive instead. I can simply plug in the Ventoy drive, load its GUI interface, and then navigate to the CLI version of this tool.

Once you load the netboot.xyz’s interface, you need to configure the network connection. I thought it would pick up Ethernet effortlessly, but I didn't have success with it. So, I had to manually set up the connection with all the details, like IP address, subnet mask, DNS, and gateway, to make the connection usable. Only then did the tool’s interface load the necessary options, including the ability to boot from a local drive.

I use Rescuezilla to swap between operating systems and I love it

Distro hopping just got a lot easier.

12
By  Simon Batt

It divides the page into four categories. The first is booting from the local HDD, which takes you directly to the currently installed OS. Next is the distribution category, which lists Linux distributions, Live CDs, BSD, Unix network installs, FreeDOS, and Windows. I mostly deal with Linux distributions and use that option because it lists a range of options. There are two dozen Linux distributions to choose from, including the popular ones like Debian, Fedora, Kali Linux, and a lot more.

But that’s not all! Netboot.xyz understands that ISOs are not enough, and you need to have a few tools as well. GParted, MemTest86+, Clonezilla, and ShredOS are tools that must be on any rescue USB. In fact, I have most of the tools listed on its list on my Ventoy drive, and their ISO files take up a lot of storage space. As a result, I’ve deleted all the common ones from my Ventoy drive and only keep Hiren’s BootCD PE on the Ventoy drive.

Seamless OS installations

Network speed plays a crucial role

I installed many distros using netboot.xyz, and it takes a bit longer to complete than your standard installation. Since it has to fetch the files and additional resources from multiple repositories and then copy them to your machine, your internet speed plays an important role. You might not notice it while installing something as small as Tiny Core Linux. I installed Debian, and it took around 45 minutes to complete on a virtual machine.

I also tested the same installation on an old laptop with an HDD and Ethernet connections, and the results were similar. The tool can work with 1GB or more of memory. However, its official page also mentions that the requirement can exceed 4GB for some rescue environments with a GUI. I mostly stick to the Linux distribution options. You have to add a download URL to install Windows, which is a bit inconvenient.

Ventoy made testing operating systems a breeze

It's a whole new world

6
By  João Carrasqueira

Instead, I prefer keeping Windows 11 and 10 and the MX Linux ISO on the Ventoy drive, and use netboot.xyz mostly for mainstream distros like Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora. This approach saves quite a bit of storage space that was previously occupied by tools and Linux ISOs. My main reason for keeping one Linux ISO is to mitigate network problems. In case of a network outage or misconfiguration, I can still use some troubleshooting tools included with most Linux distros.

Reduce the load on your Ventoy drive

I finally have a tool that can help me keep the Ventoy drive free for other things like live persistence. Netboot.xyz covers a diverse range of tools and ISOs and is very easy to use once you set up a proper network connection. Memory isn't an issue when installing most of the distros or tools listed. You can even host your personal iPXE server with netboot.xyz locally and keep a copy of a few distros on it. I prefer downloading ISOs from its sources because they are the latest versions.

Netboot.xyz

Netboot is a PXE server that lives in the cloud.

See at Official Site
